A brief transition indicates that insertion will be the next B+-tree operation.
Lookup repeatedly applies the page-level routing rule until it reaches a leaf. The professor then asks whether the binary search performed inside each wide page can itself be optimized.
This fragment introduces the motivation for faster within-page search.

Binary search needs only about ten comparisons among 1,000 entries, but those comparisons touch unpredictable positions and branches. Random positions can miss in the CPU cache, and a near-50/50 branch direction is difficult to predict. Thus even logarithmic in-page search has hardware costs. The following optimization removes unpredictable control flow rather than changing the asymptotic number of comparisons.

Branch-free binary search replaces the data-dependent branch that chooses the left or right half with arithmetic or a conditional-move instruction. It still halves the candidate range each iteration, but avoids repeated branch mispredictions, which can be costly on out-of-order CPUs. The professor also warns against computing the midpoint as (left+right)/2 because the addition can overflow; use left+(right-left)/2. For page-sized arrays—typically thousands of entries—the branch-free form can outperform conventional binary search despite doing similar logical work.

Interpolation search uses numeric separator bounds learned during traversal to guess where a key should lie within a page. If values are roughly uniform, the proportional position of the search key in the key range predicts its array position. From that guess, exponential search expands outward until it brackets the key, then binary search finishes in the much smaller interval. A good guess beats starting at the midpoint; skew reduces the benefit but preserves logarithmic fallback behavior. This optimization depends on ordered numeric data and is not generally available for arbitrary strings.

If the data distribution is skewed, interpolation gives a poorer initial guess. The subsequent exponential and binary searches still bound the lookup cost, so skew mainly removes the speedup rather than breaking correctness.
This short interval closes the optimized-lookup example.
The lecturer notes the time limit and postpones insertion to the next recording.

Lookup deserves disproportionate optimization effort because queries perform it frequently and updates begin by locating the target leaf. A B+-tree limits the number of pages visited, but each page still contains a substantial sorted array. Efficient indexing therefore has two levels: a shallow page hierarchy and fast search within each page. Exam answers should not stop at “B+-trees are logarithmic”; they should also discuss fanout, page size, cache behavior, and the fact that inserts and deletes inherit the lookup cost.

The new lecture recaps the B+-tree invariants: a wide multiway tree, equal leaf depth, and at least half-full non-root nodes. It also reconnects to the previous lookup algorithm before moving to updates.

Lookup descends from the root and binary-searches the wide pages it encounters. Branch-free search and interpolation are optional micro-optimizations; the underlying routing algorithm remains the same.

Insertion first performs an ordinary lookup to find the target leaf. If the leaf has room, insert the entry in sorted order. If it is full, split it into two approximately half-full pages, place the new entry on the correct side, and add a separator plus child reference to the parent. If the parent overflows, repeat the split upward. Splitting the root creates a new root and increases the height by one. This recursive split rule preserves both occupancy and equal leaf depth.

Deletion is harder because removing an entry may leave a non-root page less than half full. If a sibling with the same parent has spare entries, redistribute between the two pages and update the separator. Otherwise merge with that sibling, remove the obsolete parent entry, and repair the parent recursively if it underflows. Restricting repair to a sibling under the same parent keeps navigation local. Some systems tolerate underfull pages except when empty, but adversarial insert/delete patterns can leave permanent waste; full deletion logic preserves the occupancy guarantee.

A range scan looks up the lower bound once, then enumerates entries in order and follows next-leaf pointers until the upper bound is exceeded. This avoids returning to the root for every page. If logically adjacent leaves are also physically adjacent, the scan becomes sequential I/O and is especially fast; such physical ordering is called clustering. Updates can gradually weaken clustering because a new page created in the middle of the key range may not be allocated next to its neighbors.

A compound index treats several attributes as one lexicographically ordered key: compare the first component, then use the next component only when earlier components tie. This creates the left-prefix rule. An index on (A,B,C,D) can directly support bindings on A, (A,B), (A,B,C), or all four. Binding only B or C does not identify one contiguous index range. For example, A=5 becomes the range from (5, minimum) through (5, maximum), while B=5 alone is scattered throughout the ordering.

A secondary index may contain many duplicate user keys, which makes deleting one particular tuple difficult if the index stores only that key. The standard solution is to append the tuple identifier as a tie-breaker, indexing (user key, TID). The combined value is unique, so a known tuple can be located and removed in logarithmic time. Prefix lookup by the user key still returns all duplicates as a contiguous range. The extra TID mainly enlarges inner separators, since leaves needed the TID for tuple access anyway.

Latching only the current page is unsafe: after reading a child pointer and releasing the parent, another thread could split the child before it is latched, moving the target key elsewhere. Lock coupling prevents this race by latching the child before releasing the parent, so parent and child overlap briefly. Traversal always acquires latches from root toward leaves, giving a consistent order that avoids deadlock. Here “latch” means a short-term in-memory synchronization primitive, distinct from a transaction-level logical lock.

Insertion complicates lock coupling because a leaf split can propagate upward, reversing the usual latch direction and risking deadlock. The safe-page strategy prevents long upward propagation: while descending, split any inner page that lacks room for one more separator while its parent is still latched. Consequently, a later leaf split can affect at most the already-latched parent. The cost is splitting an inner page slightly early and wasting at most one entry of capacity—negligible when a page holds roughly a thousand separators.

With variable-length keys, the system cannot know during descent whether an inner page has space for the next separator, so the safe-page test is unreliable. A restart strategy handles this: first descend with ordinary lock coupling. If the insertion would require splitting an inner node, release the latches and restart while retaining the entire root-to-leaf latch path. This greatly reduces concurrency during the retry, but inner splits are rare—roughly multiplicative in page capacity—so the common case stays cheap and the implementation remains simple.
The lecture moves from correct lock coupling to techniques that improve its concurrency.

Lock coupling holds a parent while acquiring its child, but latching a high-level page indirectly blocks access to a vast subtree. If the desired child must be fetched from disk, unrelated traversals can wait behind that parent latch. B-link trees improve concurrency by allowing a traversal to release the parent before latching the child. A concurrent split may then move the target to the right, so every page carries a right link and a high-key boundary. If the target exceeds the page’s range, follow right links until reaching the correct page or proving absence.

Right links are needed on inner pages as well as leaves. A split can move the relevant routing interval to a newly created right sibling before the traversal arrives, so the same sideways correction must work at every level.
The board sketch illustrates following successive right-sibling pointers after a concurrent split.

B-link lookup and insertion work because splits move key ranges to the right, exactly the direction covered by sibling links. Proper deletion is much harder: redistribution or merging can move keys left and can retire a page while another thread is approaching it. Correct implementations therefore need an additional safe-reclamation mechanism, such as epochs, ensuring that a page is not removed while an older traversal may still reference it. Systems that avoid full merge-on-delete sidestep much of this complexity at the cost of weaker space maintenance.

Optimistic lock coupling removes the reader counter that would make a hot root cache line bounce among CPU cores. A reader records the page’s version, reads without taking a shared latch, and then validates that the version is unchanged and no writer is active. Writers set an exclusive bit, modify the page, increment the version, and release it. Failed validation restarts from the root. Because conflicts are uncommon, read-only inner-node traversal becomes cheap; real latches are still appropriate for leaf updates or long scans. Parent and child versions are validated in coupling order before the parent is forgotten.

Optimistic lock coupling targets high-contention inner nodes: readers validate versions instead of updating a shared latch word. The technique is newer than classical B-link or lock-coupling treatments but is important for modern multicore B-tree performance.

Bulk loading avoids performing millions of independent B-tree inserts. Repeated inserts can touch pages many times, produce random I/O, and—when keys arrive in increasing order—repeatedly split the rightmost leaf into half-full pages. Sorting the incoming data first transforms construction into sequential work. Because the loader knows it is building a new index, it can fill pages directly rather than applying the ordinary online split policy. The goal is both faster construction and dense, well-clustered leaves.

To build a fresh B+-tree, sort the records by index key and stream them into fully packed leaf pages, recording each page’s largest key as a separator. Then stream those separators into packed inner pages, again recording their largest keys for the next level. Repeat until a single page remains as the root. Every pass is sequential, nearly every page is full, and logically adjacent leaves are physically clustered. This is the ideal bulk-load outcome: minimal random I/O, high space utilization, and excellent subsequent range-scan locality.

Bulk-updating an existing tree merges sorted new records with the existing leaf stream and forms replacement pages. A naive merge would shift every later page even after the last new record. To stop rewriting, begin a new unchanged chunk once output would contain only old entries, allowing a locally underfull but valid boundary page. Propagate changed separators similarly through higher levels. This minimizes I/O but can weaken clustering and is complex; a common alternative is to drop the index, load the table, and rebuild the index from scratch.

Bulk operations are fast but disruptive because an index being rebuilt may be unavailable or unusable by queries. Partitioned B-trees trade extra query work for keeping the index online during large loads.
This interval emphasizes that layer-by-layer bulk construction temporarily leaves no complete index for normal lookup.

A partitioned B-tree prepends an artificial partition identifier to the real compound key. Existing data might use partition 0; each new bulk load receives a larger identifier and therefore appends at the right edge of the tree instead of merging into the middle. Prefix compression makes the repeated partition identifier nearly free within a page. New partitions can be created online, and background work can later merge them into older partitions. The design exchanges immediate global order for uninterrupted bulk ingestion.

Partitioning isolates new bulk-loaded runs so the main index stays online. The system should keep the number of partitions small because a point or range lookup may have to probe every partition. Background merging gradually moves entries from newer partitions into the base partition, reducing read amplification without a long offline rebuild. One or two partitions are manageable; accumulating many defeats the purpose.

Lazy merging can run in small background increments: copy a slice from a newer partition into the older one, then repeat until the newer partition disappears. Because each step rewrites only a small region, the index remains queryable throughout. The cost is temporary duplication of logical work and more complicated read reconciliation. Availability improves, but consolidation is delayed.

Partitioned B-trees lose a single global physical run: to find key x, the DBMS must search all active partitions and merge their results. That cost requires eventually consolidating partitions. Bulk deletions and updates are harder still because the base entry remains in an older partition while the new partition must record a cancellation or replacement. Reads must reconcile these records in partition order. Online availability is therefore purchased with read amplification, background merging, and more complex semantics.
A bulk deletion is represented in the newer partition as a tombstone for a tuple that still physically exists in an older partition. This deferred record must override the older value during lookup.
The literature calls these cancellation records “antimatter” entries.

A query merges results across partitions. If an older partition supplies x and a newer partition supplies a tombstone for x, the two annihilate and x is omitted. An update is handled similarly: the newer record supersedes the older version. This reconciliation is the price of applying bulk changes online. Partition order determines which information wins.

Partitioned B-trees make online bulk operations possible, but queries must merge partitions and apply updates or tombstones. That logic adds implementation complexity and runtime overhead. The structure is most attractive where continuous availability is more important than the simplicity and read performance of a single fully merged tree. It is fundamentally an availability-versus-read-cost engineering tradeoff.

Fixed-length B-tree keys make occupancy easy to express as an entry count, but real keys may be strings, compressed values, or compound encodings of variable size. Then a page can be full with few long keys or have room for many short ones, and the next separator’s size is unknown. The B-tree often treats keys as opaque byte strings plus a comparison function, so it cannot reason about their internal meaning. Slotted pages can store the bytes, but they do not restore the classical occupancy and height guarantees.

The alternating short/long-key example shows why separator choice affects height. If every leaf ends with a long key and the loader promotes that maximum as the separator, inner pages fit very few entries and the tree becomes unnecessarily deep. The leaves may be well packed by bytes, yet the inner fanout collapses. Variable-length B-trees therefore need to optimize not only page fill but also which boundary key is promoted.

By shifting leaf boundaries slightly, the loader can arrange for short keys rather than long keys to become separators. In the constructed example, that small change raises inner-node fanout enough to reduce the tree from four levels to two. The lesson is that byte occupancy and entry count are not interchangeable when key lengths vary.

Naively splitting variable-length pages can lose the familiar logarithmic bound with a useful branching factor because a poor long separator may dominate each inner page. During bulk loading, a practical strategy allows page fill to vary within a small constant range and chooses the shortest separator available in that range. Stronger dynamic algorithms exist but may rebuild parts of the index and cause performance spikes. Database implementations therefore often prefer robust heuristics over theoretically optimal but complicated maintenance.

A pragmatic split heuristic first sorts the overflowing page’s entries, then examines a window—such as 20%—around the median. It promotes the shortest key in that window, breaking ties in favor of the candidate closest to the median. This preserves reasonably balanced byte utilization while avoiding pathological long separators. Bulk loading can apply the same principle by varying page boundaries slightly to obtain shorter promoted keys. The method is heuristic, but simple and effective for typical data.
The lecture pauses after presenting the practical separator-selection heuristic.

The next recording recaps the variable-length-key problem: naive page boundaries can promote large separators and destroy fanout. The remaining B+-tree techniques aim to shorten stored keys and recover shallow trees.
The transition restates the objective: better separators increase inner-node fanout and reduce tree depth.

Because a B+-tree separator need only fall between the largest key on the left and the smallest key on the right, it can sometimes be replaced by a much shorter value that does not occur in the data. This raises fanout without changing lookup. The difficulty is constructing such a value for arbitrary opaque keys. Even strings become hard under locale-sensitive Unicode collation, where byte order and linguistic order differ and the collation mapping may not be reversible. The technique is powerful when the key domain provides a safe “between” operation, but it is not universal.

Page-prefix compression works for opaque lexicographically ordered byte strings. Neighboring keys often share a long beginning, so store that common prefix once in the page header and keep only each key’s suffix. Lookup compares the search key with the prefix, strips it when it matches, and searches the suffixes. Reconstructing full keys adds cost during output-heavy index-only scans, so some systems compress only inner nodes; nevertheless, the space saving and resulting fanout gain often justify using it in leaves too.

Prefix compression also benefits compound keys because neighboring entries frequently share the leading attributes. It pairs especially well with partitioned B-trees: the artificial partition identifier is repeated across a page and can be stored once, making its per-entry space cost negligible. For numeric keys, the byte encoding should preserve lexicographic order so neighboring numbers share leading bytes.

Big-endian encoding places the most significant byte first, so nearby integer values share a prefix: for example, consecutive values may differ only in the final byte. Little-endian encoding places the changing low-order byte first and therefore defeats byte-prefix compression. An index may thus store numeric keys in big-endian order even on a little-endian CPU. The encoding decision is about preserving useful lexicographic structure on disk, not about the machine’s native arithmetic format.
Most contemporary x86 systems are little-endian, but native byte order need not dictate index-key order. Storage encodings can be chosen for comparison and compression properties.

Little-endian has implementation conveniences, such as reading different integer widths at the same address, but those advantages are not central to an ordered index. For prefix compression, big-endian order is the useful choice.
Even on a little-endian machine, serialize numeric B+-tree keys in big-endian form when lexicographic order and common-prefix compression matter.
Converting between little- and big-endian representations is cheap on modern processors, typically using a byte-swap instruction. The compression benefit can therefore outweigh conversion cost.
This fragment closes the discussion of endian-aware key encoding.
The lecture transitions from B+-trees to hash-based indexes.
B+-trees are the general-purpose external-memory index, but they are not the only access structure. Hash indexes specialize in exact-key lookup and can outperform trees when ordering is unnecessary.

A hash table computes a hash value, maps it to a slot, and aims for expected constant-time point lookup. A search tree instead pays logarithmic cost. The word “expected” is essential: hashing depends on a good distribution and controlled collisions, whereas balanced trees provide a deterministic logarithmic height bound. Hashing is therefore attractive for equality access but comes with weaker worst-case guarantees and no inherent order.

The comparison separates tree height from actual comparisons. A red-black tree may follow dozens of scattered pointers. A B+-tree has only a few levels, but binary-searching thousands of entries on each page still performs roughly ten comparisons per level—far cheaper because of locality, yet not constant. A well-behaved hash table typically examines only one or two entries. Its limitation is specialization: it supports exact keys, not ordered ranges, and its worst case can be linear when many keys collide.
A short fragment leads into the qualifications behind hashing’s constant-time promise.
Constant-time lookup is conditional on a suitable table size, hash function, and collision behavior. When those assumptions fail, performance can degrade sharply.

A chaining hash table stores a pointer per directory slot and follows a short linked list for collisions. Keep the load factor below a chosen threshold so expected chains remain short. Mapping by h mod n is robust when n is prime because it is less likely to share a factor with patterns in a weak hash function, but integer division is costly. Power-of-two tables replace modulo with a bit mask and are fast, provided the hash thoroughly mixes the bits being used. The main lesson is that hash quality, table sizing, and slot reduction must be designed together.
The professor pauses while recalling the multiplicative constant used in Fibonacci hashing; the exact constant is not the conceptual point.
This one-word continuation completes the aside about the large hashing constant.

Fibonacci hashing is cheap but concentrates quality in the high bits, so the implementation must select those bits according to table size. Identity hashing is unsafe, while full cryptographic hashing is unnecessarily expensive. Hardware-supported CRC32 or a few AES rounds can provide a practical speed/quality compromise; portable software hashes such as MurmurHash cost more instructions. Seed the hash randomly per process or table so an attacker cannot easily construct colliding inputs. No finite hash can eliminate collisions, but good mixing and an unknown seed make pathological sets unlikely.

Production hashing requires more care than the textbook picture suggests. Hash-function selection, reduction to a slot, and hardware behavior are part of the data-structure design, not incidental details.

Chaining often incurs two cache misses: one for the slot and another for the pointed-to entry. A compact fingerprint derived from unused hash bits can be stored in otherwise unused pointer bits, allowing many unsuccessful lookups to stop before following the pointer. Open addressing stores entries directly in the table and avoids that indirection. Robin Hood hashing controls probe length by swapping in an entry that is farther from its ideal slot than the current occupant. It improves locality but is more complex, especially for parallel construction; well-engineered chaining remains a strong baseline.

In-memory hash-table techniques transfer poorly to disk. Every link in a collision chain can require another random page read, and growing a table by conventional rehashing rewrites all entries to unrelated locations. The table size is not known when a relation is created, so growth is unavoidable. External-memory hashing therefore needs a directory that can expand while preserving most existing bucket pages, avoiding a full random-I/O rebuild.

Hash indexes normally support equality only, not useful range access. This also complicates duplicate secondary keys: appending the TID makes entries unique, but querying only the original key would require a range over all TID suffixes, which hashing cannot provide. Consequently, disk hash indexes are most natural for unique keys. A hybrid can replace a long duplicate chain with a tree, but that adds substantial complexity. When duplicate or range behavior matters, a B+-tree is usually the safer choice.

Extendible hashing addresses unknown disk-table size. A too-small directory creates long collision chains; a too-large one wastes space; rebuilding every bucket is prohibitive. Instead, directory entries may share bucket pages, and overflowing buckets are split locally by considering additional hash bits. The directory can grow without relocating all existing records. Only the affected hash range is reorganized.

An extendible-hashing directory has a power-of-two number of entries. The global depth says how many hash bits index the directory; each bucket has a local depth saying how many bits actually distinguish it. When local depth is smaller than global depth, several systematic “buddy” entries point to the same bucket. This sharing is what permits one part of the hash space to split without changing unrelated buckets.
The example reaches a full bucket and prepares to split it.

On bucket overflow, allocate a second bucket, increase the overflowing bucket’s local depth, and redistribute its records using one additional hash bit. Directory entries that formerly shared the old bucket are divided between the two pages. If the directory already has enough global depth, this is only a local update: other buckets and their records remain untouched.
Before the split, multiple directory entries shared the same physical bucket. The split removes some of that sharing.

The larger example shows repeated local growth: split only the bucket that overflowed, redistribute its contents with another hash bit, and redirect only the directory entries that referenced it. An unrelated bucket remains unchanged. If no additional directory bit is available, the global directory must be expanded before this local split can occur. Local depth determines which case applies.
The next case handles a split when local depth already equals global depth.
If the overflowing bucket is no longer shared, its local depth equals the directory’s global depth; the directory cannot distinguish another bit without growing.

When local depth equals global depth, double the directory and duplicate its pointers. Then split only the overflowing bucket using the new hash bit. Buckets unaffected by the split continue to be shared by paired directory entries and are not rewritten. Directory copying is invasive, but it is far cheaper than rehashing all bucket pages because the directory contains pointers while each bucket page contains many records.
The discussion now considers the practical limit on repeated directory doubling.
Exponential directory growth cannot continue indefinitely, so the implementation needs a fallback once the maximum directory depth is reached.

At maximum depth, extendible hashing may fall back to overflow chaining. This should be rare with a good hash function, but true hash collisions or adversarial inputs cannot be resolved by looking at more bits: the values remain indistinguishable. Chaining preserves correctness, though each extra page hurts disk performance. Directory growth cannot separate identical hashes.

In the ideal case, extendible hashing needs two page accesses: one directory page and one bucket page. It grows buckets locally and avoids full rehashing. The costs are abrupt directory doubling, large jumps in space consumption, and special handling for genuine collisions. Compared with a B+-tree it can provide faster equality lookup, but it is less versatile and more dependent on hash distribution.

The recap states extendible hashing’s core idea: a hash-bit directory can gain resolution without relocating every bucket. When a bucket overflows, use another bit to split only that portion of the hash space. Directory entries may continue sharing unaffected buckets, so growth rewrites pointers and the overflowing page rather than all stored records. This contrasts with full rehashing.

Doubling introduces one more directory bit. Existing bucket pages can remain in place because duplicated directory entries initially point to the same buckets; only the overflowing bucket is redistributed.
This fragment closes the extendible-hashing recap.
The lecture turns to the abrupt-growth disadvantage of extendible hashing.

Directory doubling has acceptable amortized cost but poor latency: long quiet periods are punctuated by an operation that copies the entire directory and doubles its space. At large scales, one such step can stall the system for seconds or longer. Linear hashing is motivated by smoothing this staircase into incremental growth rather than improving the final asymptotic size.

Linear hashing retains a directory of buckets but grows it one entry at a time. Instead of doubling every slot at once, it progresses through buckets in a fixed split order. The total structure eventually reaches the same sizes as an ordinary power-of-two table, but each growth step is small, reducing disruptive latency. Growth is smoother, not ultimately smaller.
An overflowing bucket first receives an overflow page. Short chains temporarily absorb skew until a load-factor or chain-length threshold triggers the next scheduled split.

Linear hashing maintains a split pointer. When growth is triggered, it splits the bucket at that pointer—not necessarily the bucket that just overflowed—using one additional hash bit, appends the partner bucket at the end, and advances the pointer. After every bucket in the current round has split, the table has a regular doubled size and a new round begins with another bit. Thus each step adds exactly one directory entry while gradually converting all buckets to the next hash depth.
Once the split pointer reaches the end, every original bucket has been split once. The table is regular again, and the next round begins at the first bucket with one more hash bit.

Lookup computes a bucket using the current higher hash depth. If that result lies in the part of the round not yet split, fold it back to its old-depth bucket. This requires only a boundary test and simple arithmetic. The directory can therefore be in a mixed state—some buckets using one more bit—without making lookup complicated.

Linear hashing replaces extendible hashing’s doubling spikes with steady one-bucket growth and good amortized space use. Its main cost is temporary chaining. An overflowing bucket cannot be split immediately unless it is next in the prescribed order, so its overflow pages may remain until the split pointer eventually arrives. This yields smoother maintenance but potentially slower lookups during a round.
The example prepares to show that the overflowing bucket may not be the next legal split target.

If a later bucket overflows while the split pointer is still near the beginning, linear hashing must first split each preceding bucket. Those splits may free no space in the overflowing chain. Correctness is preserved by overflow pages, but performance can remain degraded until the scheduled sequence reaches the hot bucket. This explains why chaining is integral to linear hashing rather than an exceptional last resort.

The tradeoff is explicit: linear growth avoids directory-doubling pauses, while temporary overflow chains increase lookup cost. A second practical issue is allocating a directory that can grow at its end.

A conceptually contiguous, indefinitely growing directory is difficult to place on disk because later extents may already be occupied. The practical solution is a chunked directory with geometrically increasing chunks. A hash-derived position first selects the chunk—efficiently using bit operations such as counting leading zeros—then computes the offset inside it. Chunking removes the relocation problem but adds an indirection and several instructions. That overhead is negligible compared with disk I/O, though visible for an in-memory table.
The board calculation notes that chunk-address computation is acceptable for disk-resident hashing but comparatively expensive in a purely in-memory lookup.

Linear hashing is viable for external storage, but its elegant diagram hides an allocation decision. A contiguous directory wastes reserved space or eventually needs relocation; a chunked directory costs indirection and computation. Implementations must choose a point on that space/performance tradeoff, in addition to managing overflow chains and scheduled splits. The physical representation affects the promised performance.

A flat extendible-hashing directory works well under uniform hashes, but skew can make it enormous relative to the number of buckets. Repeatedly splitting one hot prefix doubles the whole directory while most entries continue pointing to a few shared cold buckets. Skew may come from a poor hash function or from true duplicate values, which no hash function can separate. When directory space dominates bucket space, the flat structure has failed to adapt locally.
Multi-level extendible hashing replaces the single flat directory with a tree of hash directories, allocating additional hash-bit resolution only along overflowing paths.
The overflowing prefix alone needs more bits; cold directory regions should not grow with it.

When one bucket overflows, replace only that directory entry with another directory page and consume more hash bits on that path. If the child directory fills, add another level. This sacrifices strict constant depth, but each directory page contains thousands of pointers, so fanout is enormous and the tree remains shallow. Only skewed regions pay the extra page access; uniformly sparse regions stay close to the root.

A naive directory tree wastes space under uniform input. Nearly every root entry eventually overflows and receives a child page, but each child may use only one bit and remain mostly empty. Those sparse pages also pollute the buffer pool. Thus the scheme solves skewed flat-directory growth but needs sharing to avoid making uniform data its worst case.
The fix is to let buddy ranges share an inner directory page rather than allocate one sparse child per overflowing root entry.
The example returns to the initial directory and follows a single overflowing prefix into a shared lower-level page.

When one buddy overflows, all buddies in the aligned group may point to the same new inner page. The overflowing range uses an additional bit, while the other ranges still effectively ignore that bit because their entries share a bucket. As more buddies overflow, they can occupy previously unused slots on the same page. Sharing therefore provides local growth without immediately allocating many nearly empty pages.
The shared inner page can itself be subdivided as a hot prefix needs still more hash bits.
A repeatedly overflowing bucket advances from five to six relevant hash bits, requiring a finer partition inside the shared page.
The next operation splits the shared page’s range.
The inner directory is divided into aligned halves so the hot range can gain another distinguishing bit while preserving buddy boundaries.

Splitting the inner page gives the hot bucket six effective hash bits, while cold buddies may still map to one shared bucket and therefore ignore the extra bits in practice. The process can repeat locally until the current hash value has consumed all pointer capacity, at which point another directory level is added. Growth follows data skew rather than a global depth.
The structure can also fold redundant buddy pages back upward.

If every entry in a child page ultimately points to the same bucket, that page contributes no distinguishing information. The parent can bypass it and point directly to the bucket, reclaiming the redundant page. This folding operation prevents cold regions from retaining unnecessary levels after buddy sharing changes. It is the inverse of local expansion.
Folding collapses the redundant child, leaving only the one additional page that contains useful local distinctions.
Because buddy boundaries are powers of two, the effective bit width and sharing group can be derived from the pointer layout rather than stored as separate metadata.

The pointer array encodes its own buddy structure. By checking increasingly distant power-of-two neighbors, lookup can determine how many entries share the same child page and therefore how many hash bits the next level receives. This needs only logarithmically many pointer checks and no per-entry depth field. Nearly the entire page can hold pointers, giving fanout close to page size divided by pointer size—higher than a typical B+-tree inner node.

Multi-level extendible hashing adapts naturally to skew, grows pages locally instead of doubling a global directory, and achieves very high fanout because sharing metadata is implicit. Its price is an extra page access for each directory level, though the tree is normally shallow. Conceptually it combines the local adaptability of a trie with page-sized hash fanout.

The structure is elegant but implementation-sensitive. Splitting, sharing, and folding must preserve aligned buddy ranges across millions of operations; a small boundary error can remain latent for a long time. This is a useful exam distinction: conceptual simplicity and small code size do not imply easy correctness when invariants are encoded implicitly. Subtle bugs may surface only after extensive growth.
The topic shifts to bitmap indexes, which target combinations of individually unselective predicates rather than unique point lookups.

A B+-tree on a low-cardinality attribute is often worse than a table scan because each value returns a large fraction of the relation. Yet combining several such predicates can be highly selective. Building a compound index for every possible attribute combination is infeasible because the number of combinations grows exponentially and query patterns may vary. Bitmap indexes solve this composability problem by indexing each low-cardinality value separately in a form that can be combined cheaply at query time.

Traditional index intersection retrieves large TID lists and must sort or hash them before fetching tuples, making it expensive for unselective predicates. Disjunction requires union plus duplicate elimination, and negation often becomes two broad ranges. Bitmap indexes instead support conjunction, disjunction, and negation with direct bit operations. Their benefit is not a faster single unselective lookup; it is inexpensive logical composition before any base tuples are fetched.

For each value in a small attribute domain, store one bitmap with one bit per tuple: 1 means that tuple has the value. Predicates combine using word-sized operations—AND for conjunction, OR for disjunction, and bitwise NOT before AND for negation. A 64-bit CPU tests 64 tuples per operation, so complex filters can be evaluated as fast sequential passes over compact bit vectors. Only the surviving tuple positions need base-table access.
The base representation costs one bit per tuple per indexed value. If tuple identifiers are not dense positions, the bitmaps also need a shared position-to-TID directory.
Dense TIDs allow bitmap position i to mean tuple i directly. Otherwise, one common array maps bitmap positions to actual TIDs and can be reused across all bitmaps.

Bitmap vectors are often sparse and compress well with run-length encoding. Query processing can intersect the compressed runs directly: skip ranges known to be all zero and apply bit operations only to literal blocks. There is no need to decompress the entire vector first. This makes arbitrary combinations of low-cardinality predicates efficient, especially in analytical workloads; selective unique keys still belong in conventional tree or hash indexes.

A small materialized aggregate stores tiny summaries—such as minimum, maximum, sum, and count—for each physical chunk. Before scanning, the DBMS may prove that no tuple qualifies and skip the chunk, prove that all qualify and omit predicate checks, or even answer a block-level aggregate directly. The method works well because physical order often follows insertion order, so dates and increasing IDs cluster naturally, and older chunks change rarely. Updates can invalidate the summary; the next scan recomputes it lazily while reading the chunk anyway.

Chunk summaries are checked before reading detailed values. If min/max settle the predicate, the chunk is skipped or accepted; otherwise normal scanning proceeds. On modification, marking the summary invalid is often cheaper than eagerly maintaining every aggregate. The first later query rebuilds it during a scan it already had to perform. This low implementation cost and potentially large I/O saving explain its popularity in analytical systems.
Even when a summary cannot prune a chunk, checking a few metadata values is almost free. When it can prune, it avoids reading or evaluating a large block, giving an excellent cost/benefit ratio.

Multidimensional indexes answer predicates over several independent dimensions, using structures such as R-trees, grid files, or KD-trees. Their fundamental limitation is the curse of dimensionality: as dimension count grows, point distances become less discriminative and a scan can beat the index. A compound B+-tree on (A,B) is still one-dimensional because lexicographic order creates one total order and supports the left-prefix rule; a true multidimensional index can constrain B independently of A. Low dimensions can work well, but high-dimensional performance requires additional distribution or workload assumptions.
The storage-and-indexing unit concludes. The next unit revisits transaction and recovery definitions briefly, then focuses on how a DBMS implements them.

Transaction support groups several reads and writes into one logical operation with a defined beginning and end. Recovery gives that operation meaning even when the DBMS, operating system, machine, or network fails at an arbitrary instant: after restart, committed work must remain and incomplete work must not leave the database inconsistent.

These topics must be designed together. A crash can occur after only part of a transaction has executed, so recovery needs to know which work committed and which work was still in flight. For exam questions, connect transactions to the user-visible promise and recovery to the internal machinery that preserves that promise.

A bank transfer illustrates why a sequence of individually valid writes must be treated as one unit. Debiting account A and crediting account B are separate physical actions, but logically they must either both happen or neither happen. A crash between them would otherwise destroy money.

Concurrency adds a second risk: another transaction may read or update the same balance while the transfer is in progress. ACID transactions let application code state the intended unit of work while the DBMS handles failure, interference, and persistence. In an exam, identify the invariant—here, conservation of the transferred amount—and show how a partial or interleaved execution can violate it.

A transaction begins explicitly with BEGIN or implicitly when a session starts work. COMMIT requests that all of its changes become permanent; success is the durability boundary. ROLLBACK or abort instead removes every change made by the transaction, restoring the observable state as if it had never run.

Commit is requested by the client and may fail—for example because of a constraint violation or insufficient storage. Abort may also be forced externally by a lost connection, cancellation, or error, so the DBMS cannot refuse it: rollback must always be implementable. That asymmetry is an important design requirement for recovery.

ACID separates four guarantees. Atomicity means all-or-nothing execution. Consistency means a correct transaction preserves declared invariants. Isolation gives each transaction the illusion that it runs alone despite real concurrency. Durability means a successful commit survives later failures.

Do not treat these as four synonyms. Atomicity and durability primarily concern what survives failure; isolation concerns interference among concurrent transactions; consistency is the application- and schema-level correctness condition that the other mechanisms help preserve. This decomposition is useful when an exam asks which guarantee a particular anomaly or crash violates.

Recovery must protect both the DBMS data structures and the transaction guarantees when a crash occurs at any point. On restart, partially executed transactions must be undone for atomicity, the recovered state must satisfy consistency requirements, and every acknowledged commit must be retained for durability.

Durability is subtle because committed pages may still be only in the buffer pool when power fails. The system therefore needs persistent recovery information before it can safely acknowledge commit. Recovery is internal and normally invisible to users, but its design is inseparable from transaction semantics; some systems even reuse recovery mechanisms to help implement isolation.

The user-facing ideas of transactions and recovery are implemented through two interacting technical areas. Concurrency control mainly protects isolation and consistency by regulating conflicting operations. Logging mainly supports atomicity and durability by retaining enough information to undo incomplete work and redo committed work.

This mapping is deliberately approximate: the components are not completely independent, and some systems use logging or versioning techniques to provide isolation as well. For exam answers, start with the usual responsibility of each component, then mention that practical implementations interleave them.

Running transactions strictly one after another is easy to reason about but wastes resources. A transaction may pause for disk I/O, execute a long query, or wait minutes for a person; serial execution would make every other user wait during that idle time.

Concurrent execution overlaps those delays and is therefore essential for throughput and responsiveness. The difficulty is that interleaved reads and writes can change results or corrupt data. Concurrency control must retain the performance benefit while making executions obey safe transaction semantics.

A lost update occurs when two transactions read the same old value, compute different replacements, and then write them in sequence. The later write overwrites the earlier one without incorporating it. Two withdrawals of 10 and 20, for example, should reduce a balance by 30, but an unsafe interleaving may retain only one reduction.

The professor then contrasts this with a dirty read: one transaction uses a value written by another transaction that has not committed. If the writer later aborts, the reader has based durable work on a value that conceptually never existed. Lost update discards a committed effect; dirty read creates a dependency on uncommitted work.

A non-repeatable read occurs when one transaction reads the same existing item twice and obtains different committed values because another transaction updated it between the reads. Even though neither observed value is dirty, the first transaction can no longer behave as if it were alone.

The effect is more serious than a surprising display. A query plan may read the same relation at different points—for example in two branches of a join—and combine snapshots that never coexisted. The result can therefore be logically inconsistent even though every individual read returned committed data.

A phantom occurs when a transaction repeats a predicate or range query and a newly committed tuple now satisfies it, so the result set gains a row. Repeating COUNT(*) can therefore return a larger number after another transaction inserts. The following slides distinguish this from rereading an existing item whose value changed.
This brief return to the non-repeatable-read diagram begins the comparison with phantoms. The distinction is completed on the next slides.
The professor poses the key comparison: although both anomalies change the result of a repeated query, a phantom is not simply a non-repeatable read. The next two intervals define the difference.

In a non-repeatable read, the object already existed at the first access. Reading that same tuple or attribute again yields a different value because another transaction changed it. The identity of the item is stable; its contents are not.

A phantom is a newly appearing tuple, not a changed value of a tuple that was already read. A repeated point lookup of an existing key can be protected by locking that row, but a repeated range query may see a row inserted later that now satisfies its predicate.

This makes phantoms technically difficult: at the first query, the future tuple does not exist and therefore cannot be locked with an ordinary row lock. Preventing the anomaly requires protection of the searched key range or predicate, not merely the rows currently returned. That is why phantom prevention is often more expensive even when the anomaly seems less dramatic.

Strictly serial execution eliminates concurrency anomalies because only one transaction can affect the database at a time, but its performance is unacceptable. The goal is therefore serializability: allow operations to interleave physically while ensuring the overall outcome is equivalent to some serial ordering of the transactions.

The phrase “some serial ordering” matters. Transactions need not execute in their arrival order, and their individual operations need not be contiguous; the DBMS only has to prevent interleavings whose observable result cannot be explained by any serial schedule. Achieving that property requires concurrency-control bookkeeping.

Recovery is the DBMS component that preserves data and transaction guarantees across errors, especially a crash that destroys volatile state. Its two high-level sources are a database snapshot, which captures a known past state, and a sequential log, which records the changes made after that snapshot.

Recovery combines these sources rather than taking a new full copy after every transaction. The snapshot supplies a restart baseline; the log supplies the history needed to reconstruct a later correct state. The remainder of the chapter explains how that simple idea handles partial writes, committed and uncommitted transactions, and uncertain disk contents.

A snapshot is a complete copy at one point in time; the log is the ordered protocol of changes afterward. Restoring the snapshot and replaying the relevant logged changes reconstructs a newer database state.

These recovery materials must not share the same failure domain as the primary database. A second disk in the same machine is insufficient against machine destruction, and a second machine in the same room may be insufficient against fire. Keeping backups and archived logs on separate systems—and ideally at another site—turns logical recoverability into practical disaster tolerance.

Media recovery starts from a surviving backup of an earlier state and rolls the database forward using the log. It does not literally rerun the original transaction programs, because they may be nondeterministic or depend on unavailable inputs. Instead, the DBMS reapplies the recorded writes or state changes.

The important distinction is between re-executing application logic and redoing its effects. A correct log contains enough information to reproduce the latter deterministically, moving the restored snapshot toward the state that existed before the medium was lost.

After a power failure, the disk image may contain an unpredictable subset of recent buffer-pool changes. Some write requests may have completed, others may not, and uncommitted updates may already have been evicted to disk. Recovery therefore cannot assume that disk equals either the old or the newest logical state.

The required restart state contains every effect of transactions that committed before the crash and none from transactions that were still active. Recovery must redo committed changes that might be missing and undo uncommitted changes that might be present. This uncertainty is the reason the log needs both transaction status and change information.

The same log information used to remove uncommitted work after a crash can implement an ordinary transaction abort. Whether rollback is requested explicitly, triggered by an error, or required during restart, the logical task is identical: reverse every effect of the transaction while leaving other transactions unchanged.
This reuse is important because rollback is not an exceptional add-on. A correct recovery design already needs a dependable undo procedure, so normal ROLLBACK can invoke that established mechanism.

Failure classes differ by what was lost and therefore by the repair required. R1 is a local abort: undo one noncommitted transaction. After volatile memory is lost, R2 restores effects of committed transactions that may be missing from disk, while R3 removes effects of noncommitted transactions that may already be on disk.

R4, or media recovery, handles loss of external storage by restoring a backup and archived log. Local aborts are routine, system crashes are occasional, and media loss should be rare but must still be planned for. A particular buffer policy can make one phase unnecessary, but the classification describes the full logical obligations.

The buffer pool separates the current logical database from the durable page image. Dirty pages are written asynchronously, so a crash can occur after a write was submitted but before the DBMS learns whether it completed. On restart, the system cannot infer from timing alone which version of a page reached disk.

A recovery algorithm must therefore be correct for both possibilities: the change may already be present or may still be absent. Later mechanisms such as log sequence numbers make redo conditional and repeatable rather than relying on uncertain I/O completion.

A no-steal buffer policy never writes a page containing an active transaction’s update. Disk therefore contains no uncommitted changes, so crash recovery does not need an undo phase for those pages. Its cost is severe: all dirty pages of active transactions must stay in memory, so a transaction cannot safely update more data than the buffer can hold.

A steal policy permits eviction of such pages and supports larger workloads with better buffer utilization. Because uncommitted data may reach disk, recovery must be able to undo it. Production systems usually accept this extra recovery complexity for performance and scalability.

A force policy writes every page changed by a transaction to durable storage before acknowledging its commit. Recovery then knows that committed data is already present, but commit may require many expensive random page writes.

With no-force, commit can succeed while changed pages remain in the buffer and are flushed later. This greatly improves performance, but a crash may erase committed updates from memory. The recovery log must therefore support redo. Do not confuse no-force with weak durability: durability is still promised; it is achieved through the log rather than immediate data-page writes.

Buffer policy determines recovery work. Force eliminates redo because committed pages were flushed; no-force requires redo because committed changes may remain only in volatile memory. No-steal eliminates undo because uncommitted pages never reach disk; steal requires undo because they may.

The common high-performance combination is steal plus no-force, which requires both undo and redo. It decouples page replacement from transaction completion and makes commit cheap, but shifts the burden to logging and restart. In an exam, derive the required phase directly from the possibility each policy allows.

Update-in-place overwrites each page at its fixed disk location, saving space but making recovery responsible for old and new states. Twin-block storage keeps two complete copies and switches which copy is current at commit; shadow paging copies only changed pages, reducing duplication but complicating pointer management and clustering.

Update-in-place also risks a torn write: a crash may leave one page partly old and partly new. Hardware with protected write caches can provide atomic page writes. Software alternatives detect mismatched page markers and request media recovery, or first force a recoverable copy of the intended write elsewhere and then update the real page. The latter survives a partial write but doubles I/O.

The remainder of the recovery discussion assumes the demanding but performant configuration used by many DBMSs: steal, no-force, update-in-place, and fine-grained locking. Because uncommitted changes may reach disk and committed pages may remain only in memory, the protocol must support both undo and redo.

ARIES is a widely used recovery protocol that records database changes sequentially. Each relevant log record carries enough information to redo a change during restart and to undo it when a transaction aborts or is found uncommitted after a crash.

The professor highlights an intentional asymmetry called physiological logging: redo identifies the affected page and repeats the concrete change, while undo describes how to reverse the operation logically. This lets recovery reproduce page state efficiently while still reversing actions correctly even as physical organization evolves.

Every database change is reflected in both the buffer pool and a log buffer. The log buffer is flushed to the local log file, which supports fast transaction rollback and system-crash recovery. The data pages themselves can be written independently under the buffer manager’s policy.

For catastrophic media loss, local files are not enough. Database backups and archived copies of the log must be stored safely elsewhere; recovery restores the backup and replays the archived history. Local recovery is optimized for speed, whereas archive recovery prioritizes survival of an entire machine or storage device.

The in-memory log is naturally a ring buffer: transactions append records at one position while a flusher writes older records to disk and releases that space. The writer must never catch the flusher, because that would overwrite log data that has not yet become durable.

Wraparound complicates serialization when one variable-length record crosses the physical end of the array. A useful implementation maps the same physical memory twice into adjacent virtual-address ranges. Code can then write the record contiguously across the apparent boundary, while both ranges still refer to the same underlying ring. Only the final pointer needs to be normalized.

Write-ahead logging imposes two ordering rules. Before acknowledging a transaction’s commit, every log record needed to reproduce its changes must be durable. Before writing a dirty data page, every log record describing changes already represented on that page must also be durable.

A normal write system call may return while data remains in an operating-system or device cache. “Forcing” the log therefore requires a durability barrier such as write followed by fsync, not merely submitting the bytes. If power fails afterward, recovery can always redo a committed change or undo an uncommitted page update from the surviving log.

Storage devices write fixed-size sectors or blocks rather than arbitrary individual bytes. Appending a short log fragment may therefore rewrite the final sector, and a crash during that rewrite could destroy older, already durable log records in the same sector. Padding a forced log write to a complete device block avoids exposing committed history to that partial overwrite.

The block size should come from the device interface or be covered conservatively by aligned power-of-two writes. Hardware with power-protected caches can make sector writes atomic; otherwise the software must anticipate and test this rare failure path. Recovery correctness depends on these low-level details precisely because crashes can occur at the worst possible instruction.

At the crash boundary, a winner transaction is one whose commit record became durable before failure; its effects must be present after restart. A loser transaction was still active or had not durably committed, so its effects must be removed.

Recovery must leave the database observationally equivalent to a history in which all winners completed and all losers never happened. Whether some of their pages happened to reach disk before the crash does not change this classification.

ARIES restart has three phases. Analysis scans forward to reconstruct transaction state and identify winners and losers. Redo then “repeats history,” replaying necessary actions from both groups so that pages and structural changes match the instant of the crash. Undo finally walks losers backward and reverses their logical effects.

Redoing losers is essential because their physical actions may have enabled later committed work. An uncommitted B-tree insert might trigger a page split, after which a winner inserts into the new page. Skipping the loser’s split would make the winner’s logged action impossible to place correctly. Repeating history first repairs the physical structure; logical undo can then remove only the loser’s data.

The restart order is fixed: analyze the log forward, redo needed changes from winners and losers forward, then undo only loser transactions backward. The direction of each pass follows its purpose—chronological reconstruction first, reverse-order rollback last.

A change log record identifies its position with a monotonically increasing LSN, the responsible transaction, the affected page, redo and undo information, and that transaction’s previous LSN. Implementations often use the record’s byte offset as its implicit LSN. PrevLSN forms a per-transaction backward chain, avoiding a full log scan during rollback.

ARIES favors page-oriented redo and logical undo. Redo can describe a whole after-image or a smaller modification, but each record affects one known page. Undo expresses the inverse operation, such as removing an inserted key wherever it now resides. That distinction matters when later structural changes move a record to another B-tree page.

During redo, cross-page structures may still be inconsistent because recovery has not yet repaired every page. A redo operation must therefore be executable using one identified page without trusting an index traversal or another page that might still be stale.

After redo has repeated history, the physical database structures are valid again even though loser data remains. Undo can then use logical operations—such as traversing a B-tree to find and remove a key—because the index is safe to navigate. This timing explains why ARIES requires physical or physiological redo but permits logical undo.

The LSN uniquely orders log records and is commonly represented by the record’s byte offset, which grows naturally as the log is appended. The transaction ID associates each record with its transaction so analysis and undo can reconstruct that transaction’s history.

PageID names the single page affected by a redo record. A multi-page operation such as a B-tree split must therefore emit one record per page, allowing restart to repair each page independently without assuming the structure is already navigable.

PrevLSN points directly to the preceding record of the same transaction. It is logically redundant because a backward scan could eventually find that record, but the pointer makes rollback proportional to the transaction’s own number of changes instead of the size of the interleaved global log. This supports fast logical undo while redo remains page-local.

The example turns transaction actions into log records. BEGIN records establish each transaction; reads generate no record because they do not change persistent state. Each write records its LSN, transaction, page, forward action, inverse action, and PrevLSN—for example, decreasing A by 50 is undone by increasing A by 50.

A COMMIT record marks a transaction as a winner. If analysis reaches the end without a durable commit for another transaction, that transaction is a loser and its chain must be undone. The example also shows why the global log can interleave transactions while PrevLSN preserves each transaction’s private backward history.

Analysis scans the log in chronological order and reconstructs the set and state of transactions. Seeing BEGIN makes a transaction active; a durable COMMIT makes it a winner. An explicit abort or reaching the crash without commit makes it a loser.

This classification drives the later phases: winner effects must survive, while loser effects must ultimately be removed. The decisive evidence is the durable log, not what the client may have intended or what data pages happen to contain.

Redo scans forward and repairs the database to its exact crash-time physical state. Because the system uses no-force, committed changes may be missing; because updates can span pages, a structural operation may be only partly present. The log contains the complete ordered history needed to finish those changes.

Each data page stores the LSN of its newest applied change. For a log record with LSN r, recovery applies it only when the page’s LSN is older than r, then advances the page LSN. This test makes redo idempotent: a change already on disk is skipped, while a missing change is applied exactly once.

A redo action such as “decrease A by 50” is not safe to repeat blindly. If the page LSN is below the action’s LSN, the update is missing and must be applied; if the page LSN is equal or newer, the page already incorporates it and recovery skips it.

When redo finishes, the database has been physically reconstructed to the state at the crash: every data structure is valid and every logged action that had occurred is represented. Processing can now rely on indexes and other structures while the undo phase removes loser transactions.

Undo removes every remaining effect of loser transactions. Analysis remembers each active transaction’s last LSN; rollback follows PrevLSN links backward, reversing one operation at a time. Transactions whose abort completed before the crash need no further work.

Each reversal is itself logged as a compensation log record. That record describes how to redo the undo if another crash occurs, so recovery never forgets rollback progress. Logging the repair is what makes restart safe under repeated failures rather than assuming recovery will run uninterrupted.

Restart must be idempotent: rerunning redo or undo after another failure must converge to the same correct database state. Repeated crashes are realistic when the underlying fault—such as an unstable power supply—persists while the DBMS repeatedly attempts recovery.

ARIES also bounds the amount of recovery logging. A failed restart must not append the same undo work indefinitely, because that could fill the log volume and create a second failure. Page LSN tests and compensation records record which repairs are already reflected and where undo should resume.

When undo reverses a loser’s action, it appends a compensation log record (CLR) containing the positive action that performs that reversal. The CLR also stores UndoNextLSN, pointing past the action just compensated to the next original action that still needs undo.

If recovery crashes, the next redo pass reapplies the CLR only if needed, and the next undo pass follows UndoNextLSN rather than undoing the same original action again. Thus one CLR is created per reversed action, with fresh increasing LSNs, and repeated restart does not cause unbounded log growth.

After restart, the original interleaved log is followed by CLRs for each loser action that was reversed. A CLR states the redoable compensating change—for example, increasing A by 100 to reverse an earlier decrease—and identifies the next original LSN to undo.

A CLR has no inverse operation because recovery never undoes an undo. On a subsequent crash, it may redo the compensating change, then resume with UndoNextLSN. A final completion record indicates that the loser has been fully removed and no earlier operation remains.

A CLR contains a new LSN, transaction ID, affected page, redo information for the compensating action, and UndoNextLSN. It deliberately contains no undo information: compensation is durable progress and must never itself be rolled back.

PrevLSN may also be retained to preserve the complete transaction-log chain and simplify debugging, although UndoNextLSN is the field recovery actually needs to continue rollback. An implementation can combine the roles, but keeping both makes log validation and traversal clearer.

Compensation records also support partial rollback within a live transaction. The transaction can establish a savepoint, perform several later operations, then reverse only the operations after that savepoint and continue with new work. Earlier effects remain part of the transaction.

The log therefore preserves both the original actions and CLRs for the reversed subset. Logically, only the surviving prefix and later replacement actions matter, but retaining the full history makes the process restart-safe. SQL ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is an application-visible use of the same undo machinery.

Without checkpoints, analysis and redo may scan the entire log and touch many pages after every crash. A checkpoint records enough current state—especially active transactions and later, dirty-page information—to let restart begin from a more recent safe position.

A checkpoint is an interval rather than an instantaneous event because collecting and writing its metadata takes time while transactions may change state. Recovery distinguishes the checkpoint’s beginning and end, then examines only transactions whose lifetimes or changes could cross the relevant boundary.

A transaction-consistent checkpoint waits until no transaction is active and flushes dirty pages. Restart can begin analysis, redo, and undo after that point, but finding a globally idle moment may stall a busy system.

An action-consistent checkpoint briefly pauses all transactions, records which are active, and flushes dirty pages. Analysis and redo can start at the checkpoint, but undo may need to follow an active transaction’s history farther back to its minimum LSN. This reduces restart work while still imposing a stop-the-world pause, motivating fuzzy checkpoints.
This one-word interval completes the preceding point: action-consistent checkpoints can be difficult to implement without disrupting a continuously busy system.

A fuzzy checkpoint begins by recording the current recovery state while normal transaction processing continues. Dirty pages may be written during the checkpoint, but new updates may also occur, so the checkpoint summarizes a moving system rather than freezing an instantaneous database image.

With a fuzzy checkpoint, analysis can start at the checkpoint because it records the transactions active there. Redo starts from the minimum recLSN among dirty pages: the earliest logged change that might not yet be reflected on disk. Undo may need to reach the minimum LSN of any active loser transaction.

This increases restart bookkeeping compared with a quiescent checkpoint, but the DBMS never has to stop normal work. Commercial systems accept the more complex recovery boundaries because avoiding a global pause is far more important during normal operation.

A fuzzy checkpoint need not force every dirty page. It records the dirty-page table, including the earliest LSN whose change for each page may still be absent from disk. The minimum of those recLSNs bounds how far redo must scan backward.

A frequently modified page can keep that minimum very old and make restart expensive. The DBMS may proactively flush such a page—not for correctness of the checkpoint, but to advance its recorded page LSN and shorten future recovery. Fuzzy therefore means “not necessarily forced,” not “never written.”

This interval closes the recovery chapter and introduces set-oriented query processing. The focus now moves from preserving correct storage and transactions to executing analytical queries efficiently.

Record-at-a-time code is easy to write but can produce quadratic work. A naive intersection that compares every element of one million-row list with every element of another examines an impossible number of pairs.

Set-oriented processing sees the complete inputs and can invest in global organization. Sorting both lists costs O(n log n), after which a merge-style intersection is linear. Database operators use this perspective because the cost of preprocessing is amortized across millions or billions of tuples, transforming a simple but unscalable nested loop into a scalable algorithm.

Working on a whole relation makes preprocessing worthwhile: an operator can sort, hash, build an index-like structure, partition data that exceeds memory, or distribute partitions across workers. The setup cost would be wasteful for one tuple but is amortized over a large input.

The tradeoff is implementation complexity. The concise nested loop is easy to understand, whereas scalable algorithms require memory management and richer control flow. Database execution engines deliberately accept that complexity once so every query can reuse the efficient operator.

A query plan is represented as relational-algebra operators. A scan produces tuples from a stored relation, a selection filters them, and a join combines two inputs. Each operator consumes zero or more relations and conceptually produces one relation, allowing plans to form trees.

SQL execution is actually bag-oriented rather than pure set-oriented because relations may contain duplicate tuples unless a constraint removes them. Operators must preserve or eliminate duplicates according to SQL semantics. This difference often changes both correctness rules and algorithmic cost.
This brief interval poses the implementation question: how can generic relational-algebra operators execute efficiently when the future query and its data types are not yet known?

The lecture pauses after introducing the algebraic model. Before continuing, students are expected to review the meanings of the standard relational-algebra operators; the next lecture focuses on how those familiar logical operators are implemented efficiently.
The new recording resumes the discussion of set-oriented query processing introduced at the end of the recovery lecture.

The core motivation is scale: processing a relation as a large set lets the DBMS choose algorithms that exploit global structure, instead of repeatedly handling isolated items with expensive pairwise logic.

Sorting, hashing, and indexing have setup costs, so they pay off only when reused across many tuples. Set-oriented execution amortizes that investment and is the foundation for scalable database algorithms.

SQL is compiled into a tree of relational-algebra operators. In the example, scans read base relations, a selection keeps lectures with the desired title, and joins connect students, attendance records, and lectures. Intermediate relations are conceptual interfaces; the engine need not materialize every one.

Each operator consumes relations and produces a relation, which makes operators composable. Because SQL normally uses bag semantics, equal tuples can occur multiple times and multiplicity must be respected. An exam answer should distinguish the logical operator tree from the physical choice of how each operator is executed.

The lecture now moves from the logical algebra to reusable implementation strategies. Before studying individual operators, it establishes how one operator implementation can remain valid for arbitrary future queries.

The board separates three times: the DBMS software is compiled, a particular SQL query is compiled much later, and that query is executed later still. At DBMS-build time, developers cannot know the customer’s future schemas, types, predicates, or tuple layouts.

Physical operators must therefore be query-agnostic frameworks. Query compilation supplies the missing query-specific behavior, and execution invokes that behavior on actual tuples. Keeping these times distinct explains why operators use callbacks or generated code instead of hard-coding a particular comparison or field access.

A generic intersection operator can be parameterized by subscripts: functions that supply the left input, supply the right input, and compare one element from each side. With comparison alone, it can sort both sides and merge them without knowing whether tuples contain integers, strings, or many attributes. A hash-based version would additionally receive compatible hash functions.

Even tuple size can sometimes remain unknown by sorting arrays of pointers rather than moving tuple bytes. The operator owns the reusable data and control flow; the subscripts supply query-specific meaning. This separation lets one tested implementation handle arbitrary schemas.

An algebraic operator defines abstract control and data flow: when to request input, how to organize it, and when to call helper functions. It treats tuple contents as opaque. Query-specific details—attribute access, predicates, comparison, hashing, and result construction—live in subscripts attached during query compilation.

This abstraction produces fully generic operators that work for varied schemas and types. Specialized variants may use metadata such as fixed tuple width to improve sorting or copying, but the engine still needs a fallback that assumes almost nothing. EXPLAIN VERBOSE exposes these otherwise hidden parameters in a concrete plan.

Intersection of two sorted inputs uses two cursors. Compare the current tuples: if they are equal, emit the value; if the left value is smaller, advance only the left cursor; otherwise advance only the right. No value skipped on the smaller side could match the larger current value.

The algorithm is linear after sorting and remains schema-independent. The input providers and three-way comparison are supplied as subscripts, so the loop need not know tuple width, attribute count, or data type. Its correctness follows from sorted order, not from the representation of the values.

Operators exchange a common abstraction: a relation, bag, or—most generally—an ordered stream of tuples. Stream is the broadest term because operations such as ORDER BY and LIMIT make tuple order observable, while ordinary SQL also permits duplicate values.

An operator assumes only that its children can produce the expected tuple stream, not whether that stream comes from a table scan, filter, join, grouping, or another subtree.
